paper_title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Foundation models, which rely primarily on the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), have achieved impressive performance in wide range of areas such as natural language processing (NLP, Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023), computer vision (Siméoni et al., 2025), time series forecasting (Ilbert et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2023), and mathematical reasoning (Comanici et al., 2025). These models are typically pretrained on massive amounts of diverse data (Du et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025) to encode general knowledge in their weights. common use of foundation models is as frozen feature extractors, which provide rich representations for downstream tasks without retraining or finetuning the model (Lee et al., 2025; Oquab et al., 2024; Roschmann et al., 2026). Probing intermediate representations. standard way to evaluate representations is through linear probing: the model is frozen, and linear classifier is trained on top of the representation. Alain & Bengio (2017) introduced probing as diagnostic tool for neural networks and observed that classification accuracy increases with depth. Their experiments, however, focused on supervised, task-specific convolutional neural networks (CNN, LeCun et al., 1998). While the final layer may be optimal for model trained for single task, it need not be for model trained to generalize across tasks. Recent work shows that intermediate layers of LLMs can outperform the final layer across diverse downstream tasks (Skean et al., 2025). For VFMs, however, the picture is less clear. Skean et al. (2025) report that intermediate layers are beneficial in autoregressive VFMs (El-Nouby et al., 2024; Fini et al., 2025), while final representations remain optimal in non-autoregressive models such as ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024). In contrast, Bolya et al. (2025) find that intermediate layers provide the best embeddings in contrastive VFMs, and Uselis & Oh (2025) observe similar trend in ViT, particularly under distribution shift. This motivates further investigation. Layer by layer, module by module. The layer-wise analyses discussed above share common limitation: they all treat the transformer block as an atomic unit. This perspective overlooks the intermediate representations produced within each block, illustrated in Figure 2, namely the outputs of normalization layers, attention modules, feedforward linear layers, activation functions, and residual connections.1 These components can exhibit distinct properties, notably in terms of smoothness and adaptability during finetuning (Odonnat et al., 2026). We therefore conduct large-scale, systematic study of transformer representations in VFMs and LLMs, layer by layer, module by module. We ask two natural questions: 1) How much can optimal representations improve over standard probing? and 2) Can simple fixed heuristic recover most of the gain at no extra cost? Our contributions. We conduct extensive experiments on VFMs and LLMs. Figure 1 illustrates our findings, showcasing the suboptimality of probing the final-layer residual stream and the joint importance of both layer and module choices. Our main contributions can be summarized as: 1. Layer and module choices matter jointly. Probing the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than probing the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across depth, showing that layer and module choices should not be considered independently. 2. Practical benefits. We evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for VFMs and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for LLMs. Both strategies improve performance in majority of evaluations and recover substantial fraction of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair. 3. Impact of transfer difficulty. When the discrepancy between pretraining and downstream data is large, transfer becomes more difficult. For VFMs, we find that the benefits of optimal probing locations increase in such settings, with Act@100 yielding larger gains. Moreover, the impact of depth grows under distribution shift, allowing further improvement through the best layer-wise Act representations. 1In what follows, we use the terms block and layer interchangeably, as well as module and component, referring to normalization layers, multi-head attention modules, feedforward layers, activation functions, and residual connections throughout the network.

sections.title: 2 PROBING TRANSFORMERS LAYER BY LAYER, MODULE BY MODULE
sections.content: FC2 FFN FC1 FC2 LN2 FFN + RC2 + RC2 σ Act Act The transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) consists of successive transformer blocks, each taking as input sequence of tokens (x1, . . . , xn). As shown in Figure 2 (left), each block is made of alternating multi-head attention modules (MHA), with self-attention for encoders and causal attention for decoders, and feedforward networks (FFN). standard FFN consists of two linear transformations, denoted FC1 and FC2, separated by non-linear activation function Act, such as GELU (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016). Assuming the pre-norm standard (Xiong et al., 2020), two normalization layers (LayerNorms (Ba et al., 2016) or RMSNorm (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019)), respectively LN1 and LN2, precede the attention and feedforward blocks, and two residual connections, respectively RC1 and RC2, follow them. We will refer to RC2 as the residual stream, i.e., the output of the transformer block. In this work, we track the outputs of these eight sequence-tosequence operations at each layer, indexing them by layer-module pair (ℓ, m). Some large-scale transformers replace the standard two-layer FFN with gated FFN. It combines the non-linear projection with an additional linear projection through element-wise multiplication. To ensure consistency between standard and gated FFNs, we recover the FFN representations as follows: FC1 is the linear layer fed as input to the non-linear operation σ, Act is the non-linear transformation with gated mechanism (thus absorbing the additional linear projection), fed as input to the second linear function, and FC2 is this second linear projection. This is illustrated in Figure 2, with exact tensor definitions deferred to Appendix B.1. Figure 2: Transformer representations. We probe transformer representations (colored) across layers in VFMs and LLMs, covering models with standard (left) and gated FFN (right). + RC1 + RC1 LN1 MHA MHA LN LN2 FC3 FC1 σ Evaluating transformer representations. Following Oquab et al. (2024) and Muennighoff et al. (2023), we evaluate transformer representations via linear probing for classification (Alain & Bengio, 2017), which provides common evaluation for visual (Chen et al., 2020) and textual (Lee et al., 2025) embeddings. Each probing location (ℓ, m) produces sequence of tokens (x1, . . . , xn) (Rd)n, where ℓ denotes the relative depth expressed as percentage2, and is the transformer module being probed. By abuse of notation, denotes either the embedding dimension or the FFN hidden dimension, which is generally larger. As in Joseph et al. (2026), we embed this sequence in Rd by global average pooling over content tokens, namely image patches or text tokens; that is, special tokens, including CLS, register tokens (Darcet et al., 2024), EOS, and BOS, as well as padding positions (PAD), are masked before pooling and do not contribute to the representation. This allows us to focus on representations produced within transformer blocks, with consistent feature extraction procedure across models (e.g., AIMv2 models (Fini et al., 2025) do not use CLS token). Implementation details to ensure scalable evaluation across layers and modules are provided in Appendix B. Measuring improvement with oracle gains. The performance of the representation at location (ℓ, m) is the probing test accuracy on given dataset or benchmark, denoted by acc(ℓ, m). We use the final-layer residual stream, i.e., RC2 at 100% relative depth, as the probing baseline, denoted by RC2@100. We define the gain at location (ℓ, m) as the accuracy difference in percentage points (pp) relative to the baseline, i.e., g(ℓ, m) = acc(ℓ, m) acc(100, RC2). To disentangle the impact of depth, module, and their interaction, we analyze the following oracle gains: Glayer = max ℓ g(ℓ, RC2), Gmodule = max g(100, m), Gjoint = max ℓ,m g(ℓ, m). sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: In this section, we address the questions raised in Section 1 through large-scale evaluations of vision (Section 3.1) and language models (Section 3.2); see Appendix for the full implementation details.

sections.title: 3.1 PROBING VISION FOUNDATION MODELS
sections.content: We consider models that cover different pretraining paradigms and scales: supervised ViT models (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), discriminative self-supervised DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) and DINOv3 models (Siméoni et al., 2025), and autoregressive AIMv2 models (Fini et al., 2025). This results in total of 15 publicly available models, ranging from 22M to 7B parameters. Experiments are conducted on diverse set of 18 image classification datasets, commonly studied in the literature (El-Nouby et al., 2024; Oquab et al., 2024). Table 7 provides an overview of the datasets. Following Oquab et al. (2024), linear probing is done via logistic regression, with features preprocessed using standard scaler. The performance of given representation is its top-1 test accuracy at the dataset level (%). Overall, VFM experiments comprise nearly 90 000 probing evaluations. Optimal representations yield substantial gains. We first analyze the oracle gains provided by the best probing locations across depth and modules. Figure 3 displays the complementary cumulative distribution of gains over the probing baseline. Each curve shows, for given gain threshold x, the percentage of model-dataset pairs with gain greater than when probing the best representation over layers alone (Glayer), modules alone (Gmodule), or both jointly (Gjoint). We observe consistent gains, reaching up to 10 pp with Gjoint Gmodule Glayer across the distribution. The first inequality follows directly from Eq. (1), while the second highlights the importance of module choice, which is often overlooked in prior work. Moreover, the gap between Gjoint and Gmodule demonstrates the additional benefit of jointly selecting layers and modules. Towards fixed probing strategy. Ideally, we would like to identify probing location at fixed layer-module pair that recovers part, if not all, of the gain. We first examine how often each module appears in the best layer-module pair achieving Gjoint. We find that Act is optimal for 64.8% of the 270 model-dataset pairs, compared with 9.3% for LN2, the next most frequent, and 5.9% for the baseline module RC2 (full results in Table 15). This suggests that it is good candidate for the fixed Figure 3: Substantial gains from optimal probing locations in VFMs. Complementary cumulative distribution of gains over the probing baseline across 270 model-dataset pairs (each defining run) when using the best representation across layers (Glayer), modules (Gmodule), or both (Gjoint). Figure 4: Impact of Act and intermediate layers in VFMs. Probing accuracy across layers for Act and RC2 on Cifar10, Sketch, and Quickdraw. Results are reported for the 307M-parameter variant, common to each model family. The star indicates the best Act performance over depth.

The same phenomenon occurs in DINOv3, despite its classification performance being reported to increase smoothly towards the final layers (see Siméoni et al., 2025, Section 6.2.1). These observations hold across model sizes, as shown in Figures 15 to 26. The interaction between layers and modules is illustrated in Figure 1 (left), which displays the frequency with which each layer-module pair achieves the oracle gain Gjoint across 270 model-dataset pairs. They are small on easy datasets such as Flowers102 and Pets, which are typically included in pretraining datasets (see Oquab et al., 2024, Table 15), but more pronounced on challenging benchmarks. We discuss this in the next paragraph. Gain increases with transfer difficulty. Linear probing evaluates the transferability of frozen representations on downstream data. We therefore define the empirical transfer difficulty of dataset as the mean probing error (%) of the baseline across all evaluated models, with higher values indicating more difficult transfer from pretraining to downstream data. Figure 6a shows that the oracle gain Gjoint is positively correlated with transfer difficulty (Spearman ρ = 0.87, p-value < 0.001). This trend is illustrated by Cifar10, Sketch, and Quickdraw, which progressively depart from natural-image statistics: Figure 14 shows that the benefits of intermediate depth and alternative modules increase with transfer difficulty on these representative datasets. Our finding at the level of individual representations is consistent with Head2Toe (Evci et al., 2022), which shows that aggregating intermediate representations provides larger gains for target domains farther from the pretraining domain. We then consider controlled distribution shifts, following the evaluation protocol of DINOv3 (see Siméoni et al., 2025, Section 6.2.1). We train the classifier on features extracted from Cifar10 and evaluate it on corrupted test set from Cifar10-C over 5 corruption types (Contrast, Gaussian Noise, Motion Blur, Snow, Speckle Noise) and increasing severities in {1, 3, 5}. As shown in Figures 6b and 6c, the oracle gain Gjoint increases with corruption severity, while the optimal depth decreases. This suggests that the benefits of intermediate layers increase with distribution shift. To further investigate when these representations (a) Transfer difficulty. (b) Corruption severity. Before finetuning, accuracy curves are concave when pretraining and downstream data differ substantially, with intermediate representations achieving the best performance. After finetuning, the curves straighten, with performance increasing monotonically towards the final layers. Finally, Figure 6d shows that oracle gains decrease with pretraining scale, computed as the number of tokens seen during pretraining (see Appendix C.1.2 for details). The relative error reductions follow the same order, with 15.7% for ViT, 12.1% for DINOv2, 10.8% for AIMv2, and 7.6% for DINOv3. This is consistent with Figure 6a. Model size, in contrast, has no significant effect on gains; see Appendix C.1.6 for details. We note that these findings are observational, not causal, since many confounders exist in our analysis (architectural differences, training objectives, quality and diversity of pretraining data).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Takeaway 1. For VFMs, the best probing locations across layers and modules yield substantial performance gains. The simple fixed strategy Act@100 improves performance in majority of evaluations, recovering nearly half of these gains at no extra cost. Layer and module choices become more important as the discrepancy between pretraining and downstream data increases, while near-in-distribution datasets tend to benefit less from changing the probing location.

sections.title: 3.2 PROBING LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
sections.content: We now extend our analysis to large language models. As in Skean et al. (2025), we consider generalpurpose LLMs: Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), Llama3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma3 (Gemma Team et al., 2025), for total of 9 publicly available models, ranging from 1B to 12B parameters. Following prior work on textual embeddings (Lee et al., 2025; Li & Zhou, 2025; Skean et al., 2025; Tang & Yang, 2026), we use the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB, Enevoldsen et al., 2025). We evaluate using the official MMTEB implementation (available at https: //github.com/embeddings-benchmark/mteb/) via linear probing with logistic regression on 24 classification tasks from the MTEB(Multilingual) benchmark, spanning 31 languages and 14 domains. Table 11 provides an overview of the tasks. Following MTEB evaluation protocol (Enevoldsen et al., 2025), the performance of given representation is its average test accuracy across tasks (%). Overall, the LLM experiments comprise over 54 000 probing evaluations. Figure 7: Substantial gains from optimal probing locations in LLMs. Gains over the probing baseline on MTEB(Multilingual) from probing the best representation across layers (Glayer), modules (Gmodule), or both (Gjoint) in Qwen3, Llama3, and Gemma3 models. Optimal representations yield substantial gains. Figure 7 displays the gains from probing the best representation over layers alone (Glayer), modules alone (Gmodule), or both jointly (Gjoint). Gains are consistent across models and sizes, reaching up to 4 pp. Qwen3 models display larger gains than Llama3 and Gemma3 models, with the improvement increasing with model size within the Qwen3 and Llama3 families. Glayer Gmodule holds for all but one model, while Gjoint systematically exceeds both, highlighting the benefits of jointly selecting layers and modules. Towards fixed probing strategy. Similarly to Section 3.1, we aim for simple fixed probing location that improves performance. The fixed choice is simpler than for VFMs, since LN2 appears in the best layer-module pair achieving Gjoint for all but one model (see Table 19). We note that Figure 8: Impact of LN2 and intermediate layers on performance. Probing accuracy across layers for LN2 and RC2 on MTEB(Multilingual). The star indicates the best LN2 performance over depth.

For LLMs, the best probing locations across layers and modules yield substantial performance gains. The simple fixed strategy LN2@60 recovers 86.0% of these gains at no extra cost, with nearly all of the remaining gap captured by the best layer-wise LN2 representations.

sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Probing foundation models. Linear probing (Alain & Bengio, 2017; Belinkov, 2022) has become standard evaluation protocol to assess representations in foundation models across diverse modalities, including images (Chen et al., 2020; Oquab et al., 2024), text (Enevoldsen et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2023), video (Assran et al., 2025), graphs (Veliˇckovic et al., 2019), and time series (Feofanov et al., 2026; Goswami et al., 2024; Roschmann et al., 2026). Beyond linear heads, attentive probing is increasingly adopted to evaluate models with patch-level features (Chen et al., 2024; El-Nouby et al., 2024; Fini et al., 2025). While linear probes are still used, the embedding of sequences of tokens from (Rd)n to Rd is learned via an attention mechanism at the level of the sequence. The overall operation thus becomes non-linear and leads to noticeable performance improvements (El-Nouby et al., 2024). In these works, features are typically extracted from the final layer after forward pass. We challenge this convention, showing the benefits of probing intermediate representations, including within transformer blocks. Beyond probing at single location, some approaches aggregate internal representations throughout the model, combining them with learned layer weights (Peters et al., 2018), supervised feature selection (Evci et al., 2022), attention over all layers (Ciernik et al., 2026), or attention value vectors pooled across layers (Zhang et al., 2026). Our work is orthogonal to these methods: it could help identify which representations across layers and modules are worth aggregating, and, more broadly, improve our understanding of transformer representations. Understanding transformer representations. Intermediate representations can also be studied to understand what models encode rather than to improve downstream performance. Probing intermediate text representations reveals what linguistic knowledge is captured within the model (Liu et al., 2019) and where: Tenney et al. (2019) show that BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) represents the steps of the traditional NLP pipeline in an interpretable and localizable way. Similarly, Joseph et al. (2026) use linear probes to understand where physical information becomes accessible in encoderbased video transformers, and how it is organized. Linear probes are also central to mechanistic interpretability, which aims to reverse-engineer the computations of neural networks, with strong focus on LLMs. This line of work views the transformer as set of attention and feedforward modules that read from and write to the shared residual stream (Elhage et al., 2021). Probes and interventions have thus been used to analyze attention heads (Li et al., 2023), feedforward modules (Geva et al., 2021), and the residual stream (Gurnee & Tegmark, 2024; Marks & Tegmark, 2024), where the latter can be steered to control the model behavior (Rimsky et al., 2024; Turner et al., 2024). Note that, akin to feature evaluation, the residual stream is the typical representation studied in the mechanistic interpretability literature, often referred to as residual stream activation. Beyond interpretability, Odonnat et al. (2026) analyze the smoothness of individual transformer components to determine which ones to prioritize during finetuning. Our work follows this direction of looking inside transformer blocks. Yet, the goal differs: we aim to identify which internal representations are most useful as frozen features for downstream tasks, not to reverse-engineer computations, elicit specific behavior in the model, or finetune it. We discuss additional related work in Appendix A.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: This paper investigates how useful different transformer representations are for linear probing in vision foundation models and large language models. Our extensive layer by layer, module by module analysis shows that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger performance gains than selecting the best layer with the residual stream fixed, while module performance can vary substantially across depth. Building on these findings, we identify simple fixed probing strategies, Act@100 and LN2@60 for VFMs and LLMs, respectively, that improve performance in majority of evaluations and recover large fraction of the gains from the best layer-module pair. For vision models, the benefit of Act@100 increases with transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data. These findings highlight the importance of looking beyond depth alone when probing transformer models. We hope our work can contribute to better understanding of their internal representations. Limitations and future work. Our analysis focuses on linear probing for classification and could naturally be extended to other downstream tasks and modalities, including tabular and time series foun-

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used to aid and polish the writing. They were also used to discuss research ideas and experimental design, including the experimental setups of prior work, and to assist with rapid prototyping of visualizations. The authors carefully checked all LLM-generated outputs and independently implemented and verified the final experiments, analyses, and visualizations. The authors take full responsibility for the contents of this paper.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: The goal of this work is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

sections.title: A EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: In this section, we extend the discussion of prior works related to our paper in Section 4. Better transfer of intermediate layers. Several works propose explanations as to why intermediate representations can generalize better than the final layer, especially under distribution shift. The intrinsic dimension of representations first increases then decreases with depth (Ansuini et al., 2019; Recanatesi et al., 2019), and final layers exhibit neural collapse, compressing features onto class means (Papyan et al., 2020). This phenomenon also appears, more weakly, in intermediate layers (Rangamani et al., 2023). In addition, the tunnel effect describes later layers compressing representations that are already linearly separable through intermediate layers, thus degrading out-ofdistribution performance (Masarczyk et al., 2023). Although these works mostly study task-specific deep neural networks rather than large-scale pretrained foundation models, their observations are consistent with our finding that the optimal probing depth moves to earlier layers as the shift between pretraining and downstream data grows. Intermediate representations for adaptation and embeddings. Intermediate representations can also be used to adapt pretrained models efficiently. Visual Query Tuning (Tu et al., 2023) learns queries that summarize intermediate features of vision transformers, while Wu et al. (2024) implement an efficient adaptation model that selects features using the structure of the model and adapts to task difficulty. In language, LLMEmbed (Liu et al., 2024) combines representations from several layers of lightweight LLMs for text classification. When LLMs are used as frozen embedding models, training-free methods can improve the quality of extracted features by modifying either the input, with prompts (Jiang et al., 2024), or repetitions (Springer et al., 2025), or the forward pass, by re-routing internal key-value states (Tang & Yang, 2026). The adaptation methods aggregate residual stream representations across depth, while the training-free methods read the final-layer residual stream. Both could benefit from our insights by investigating other transformer modules and, for the latter, other depths as well.

sections.content: In this section, we provide the full implementation details necessary to reproduce our results. B.1 TRANSFORMER REPRESENTATIONS IN GATED FFN In large-scale transformers (Oquab et al., 2024; Touvron et al., 2023), an increasingly common alternative to the two-layer MLP feedforward network is the use of gated activations (Dauphin et al., 2017; Shazeer, 2020). Let be the embedding dimension, (x1, . . . , xn) (Rd)n be an input sequence of tokens, viewed as matrix in Rdn, be the FFN dimension, and σ be an activation function. Let W1 Rhd, W2 Rdh, W3 Rhd be weight matrices. Denoting the element-wise multiplication by and omitting the biases for readability, the standard FFN and the gated FFN are written as follows FFN(x) = W2σ(W1x), FFNgated(x) = W2(σ(W1x) W3x). (2) The main difference is that the gated FFN combines non-linear projection with an additional linear projection through element-wise multiplication. To ensure consistency between the standard and the gated FFN, we recover the FFN representations as follows: FC1 is the linear layer fed as input to the activation function (W1x in both cases), Act is the non-linear transformation fed as input to the second linear function (σ(W1x) for the standard FFN and σ(W1x) W3x for the gated FFN), and, finally, FC2 is the output of the feedforward network (FFN(x) and FFNgated(x) in (2)). This is illustrated in Figure 2. B.2 VISION FOUNDATION MODELS This section provides details on VFMs transformer representations and the linear probing setup.

sections.content: B.2.1 TRANSFORMER REPRESENTATIONS We recover embeddings across layers and modules with single forward pass using PyTorch forward hooks and pre-hooks. In our code, all VFMs inherit from the abstract base BaseVisionModel displayed in Figure 10. The feature extraction is done with the get_embeddings method. The most important abstract method to implement is block_adapter, which defines the 8 representations to extract within each transformer block. The corresponding abstract base class TransformerBlockAdapter is displayed in Figure 11. We provide below the implementation details on the VFMs used in our experiments. ViT. The Vision Transformer architecture (ViT, Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) consists of succession of transformer encoders with LayerNorms (Ba et al., 2016) and standard feedforward network with GELU activation (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016). Inputs are 2D images that are split into square patches of size , which are flattened and linearly embedded in dimension d. classification token CLS is prepended to the sequence of tokens before adding positional embeddings. The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers (Wolf et al., 2020) implementation available at transformers/models/vit/modeling_vit.py. DINOv2. The DINOv2 backbone (Oquab et al., 2024) follows the ViT architecture described above, adding LayerScale (Touvron et al., 2021) to stabilize training. All variants use standard FFN, except the 1.1B one, which uses gated FFN with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, 2020). The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers implementation available at transformers/models/dinov2/modeling_dinov2.py. DINOv3. The DINOv3 backbone (Siméoni et al., 2025) follows the DINOv2 one and implements Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE, Su et al., 2024). All variants use standard FFN, except the 7B one, which uses gated FFN with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, 2020). The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers implementation available at transformers/models/dinov3_vit/modeling_dinov3_vit.py. AIMv2. The AIMv2 model (Fini et al., 2025) pairs ViT backbone with multimodal decoder to autoregressively generate raw image patches and text tokens. In our work, we only focus on the vision part, which consists of succession of transformer encoders with RMS norms (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019) and gated feedforward network with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, Inputs are 2D images that are split into square patches of size , which are flattened 2020). and linearly embedded in dimension d. Unlike the original ViT, no CLS token is prepended to the sequence: attention is instead constrained with prefix causal mask during pretraining, enabling bidirectional attention over image patches at inference without further tuning. The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers implementation available at transformers/models/aimv2/modeling_aimv2.py. Feature extraction. Applying linear probing with logistic regression requires feeding the regressor matrix of embeddings over the entire train split (resp. test split). However, even over single batch of 512 samples, forward pass with small model like the ViT-B with 86M parameters amounts to saving 49K tensors in R768, taking around 144MiB in memory. Such an extraction over an entire dataset is thus intractable, even on high-performance GPUs like H200. To tackle this issue, we perform the probing in two steps: 1) feature extraction with embeddings saved on disk, and 2) logistic regression over frozen features. For the first step, we save each batch of pooled representations on the CPU and stream it directly to disk to maintain low GPU memory consumption and idle time, independent of the number of layers. This step is done for both the training and test samples. Then, for each (layer, module) pair, we rebuild the dataset-level embeddings over the train split (resp. test split) to fit (resp. evaluate) the logistic regression. Our implementation allows us to use logistic regression even for large-scale VFMs with up to 7B parameters. B.2.2 PROBING SETUP We conduct the probing experiments across various pretraining paradigms, model sizes, and datasets.

sections.content: images. All images are then normalized using the ImageNet1k (Deng et al., 2009) statistics. It ensures images with mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and standard deviation [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]. Note that no data augmentation is used. They are indeed not necessary since training is not stochastic: the feature extraction is deterministic, and the classifier is fitted once over all the frozen training features and evaluated once on the corresponding test features (data augmentation would, however, be required with an SGD-based linear probing (see Marouani et al., 2026)). For datasets that do not have predefined training and test sets, e.g., EuroSAT, or datasets from Cifar10-C and DomainNet, we manually create deterministic training and test sets following an 80%-20% split. The deterministic part is crucial to ensure no data leakage. Evaluation. We follow the linear probing protocol of DINOv23 by training logistic regression on frozen features for at most 1000 iterations, with L-BFGS solver, an ℓ2 penalty, and tolerance of 1e4. In our experiments, we use regularization strength = 1.0, and preprocess representations by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance with standard scaler. We ensure efficient evaluation by making use of the GPU-friendly implementation of the StandardScaler and LogisticRegression functions from the CuML library (Raschka et al., 2020). For standard evaluation, training is done on the training set of each dataset, and evaluation is done on the corresponding test set. The reported performance is the top-1 test accuracy. For the robustness analysis on Cifar10-C, akin to DINOv3 domain generalization experiments (see Siméoni et al., 2025, Section 6.2.1), training is done on the training set of Cifar10, and the learned classifier is then evaluated independently on the 15 corrupted versions of the Cifar10 test set described in the Datasets paragraph above. B.3 LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS This section provides details on LLMs transformer representations and the linear probing setup. B.3.1 TRANSFORMER REPRESENTATIONS The MMTEB benchmark (Enevoldsen et al., 2025), which expands the MTEB benchmark (Muennighoff et al., 2023) with additional domains, tasks, and languages, requires defining an encode method for given LLM, which is then used to evaluate representations over predefined set of tasks. As such, we set the desired (layer, module) pair via set_probing method, use PyTorch hooks and pre-hooks in the encode to extract representations during the forward pass, and recover the results over the corresponding set of tasks. In our code, all LLMs inherit from the abstract base BaseLanguageModel displayed in Figure 12. Abstract and hook methods are similar to BaseVisionModel (not shown due to space limitations), with an additional _load_tokenizer to load the tokenizer. The feature extraction is done with the encode method. Similarly to VFMs (see Appendix B.2.1), the most important abstract method to implement is block_adapter, which defines the 8 representations to extract within each transformer block and inherits from the base class TransformerBlockAdapter displayed in Figure 11. We provide below the implementation details on the LLMs used in our experiments. Qwen3. The Qwen3 architecture (Yang et al., 2025) consists of succession of transformer decoders with RMSnorms (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE, Su et al., 2024) and gated feedforward network with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, 2020). The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers (Wolf et al., 2020) implementation available at transformers/models/qwen3/modeling_qwen3.py. Llama3. The Llama3 architecture (Grattafiori et al., 2024) largely follows the Llama original one (Touvron et al., 2023). Similarly to Qwen3, it consists of succession of transformer decoders with RMSnorms (Zhang & Sennrich, 2019), Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE, Su et al., 2024) and gated feedforward network with SwiGLU activation (Shazeer, 2020). The checkpoints used in our experiments follow the HuggingFace transformers (Wolf et al., 2020) implementation available at transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py. 3Code available at facebookresearch/dinov2/blob/main/dinov2/eval/log_regression.py

sections.content: In this section, we provide details on the experiments in the main paper and on additional experiments. C.1 VISION FOUNDATION MODELS The results presented in this section relate to the experiments conducted on VFMs in Section 3.1. C.1.1 INTERMEDIATE LAYERS UNDER DISTRIBUTION SHIFT Skean et al. (2025) observed the benefits of intermediate layers in LLMs but not in VFMs, where performance increased towards the final layers, except for autoregressive models such as AIM (El-Nouby et al., 2024). Recent work, however, suggests that intermediate representations can also be beneficial in non-autoregressive VFMs (Bolya et al., 2025), particularly under distribution shifts (Uselis & Oh, 2025). In practice, discrepancies between pretraining and downstream data can degrade performance by making the extracted features less informative (Quiñonero-Candela et al., 2009). To illustrate this effect, we consider ViT-B (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) pretrained on ImageNet-21K and probe it before and after finetuning on downstream data. The experimental setup is described below.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Datasets. We conduct experiments on Cifar10 (Krizhevsky, 2009); 2 variants from Cifar10C (Hendrycks & Dietterich, 2019) with severity 5 (Contrast and Speckle Noise), and Flowers102 (Nilsback & Zisserman, 2008). The preprocessing follows Dosovitskiy et al. (2021) and Kolesnikov et al. (2020): for training data, we apply random cropping, 224224 image resizing, and random horizontal flip. For validation and test data, the 224224 image resizing is applied before center cropping images. All images are normalized using the ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) statistics. It ensures images with mean [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and standard deviation [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]. For Cifar10-C datasets that do not have predefined training and test sets, we manually create deterministic training and test sets following an 80%-20% split. The deterministic part is crucial to ensure no data contamination. Finetuning setup. Our finetuning experiments follow the protocol from Dosovitskiy et al. (2021) with resolution of 224 224. We optimize models with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), momentum of 0.9, no weight decay, cosine learning rate decay, batch size of 512, and gradient clipping at norm 1. For each pair of dataset-configuration, we perform sweep over 4 learning rates, as summarized in Table 12, and conduct 3 runs with different seeds relative to network initialization and dataloaders. For each run, we monitor the training using validation set (20% of the training set). The final performance is the test accuracy of the checkpoint that achieves the best validation accuracy. Results. In Figure 13, we order datasets by decreasing finetuning accuracy, using it as rough proxy for increasing distribution shift: 99.150.05 on Flowers102, 99.020.02 on Cifar10, 97.230.18 on Contrast, and 89.580.43 on Speckle Noise. We can see that the final-layer residual stream representations remain strong on near in-distribution datasets, while intermediate representations become increasingly beneficial under distribution shift. After finetuning, in contrast, performance increases monotonically towards the final layers. This shows that, akin to LLMs, intermediate representations can be effective in VFMs, and that their usefulness depends on the discrepancy between pretraining and downstream data. C.1.7 FULL RESULTS We now present the full performance comparison across all model sizes and datasets between the probing baseline RC2@100, the fixed strategy Act@100, and the oracle strategy, which probes the best layer-module pair for each model-dataset evaluation. The results in Table 17 show that Act@100 gains are broadly consistent across model sizes within most families, although some exceptions arise, most notably for ViT-B and several DINOv3 variants. The depth curves in Appendix C.1.5 provide further insight into this variation: while Act often outperforms the probing baseline RC2@100, its best-performing depth varies across model-dataset pairs and is not systematically the final layer. This effect is particularly salient for ViT-B, where intermediate Act representations often surpass RC2@100, while the final-layer Act used by Act@100 is subpar on many datasets. Further discussion on Act. Linear probing measures the linear separability of representations on downstream data. Transformer architectures preserve the representation dimensionality across layers, as the output of each block is passed as input to the subsequent block. However, different modules within transformer block can operate at different dimensionalities. In particular, residual-stream representations have the embedding dimension d, whereas FFN intermediate representations have the hidden dimension h, typically larger than (e.g., = 4d in standard FFNs). Prior work has shown that gains from feature augmentation cannot be attributed solely to increased feature dimensionality (see Evci et al., 2022, Section 3.2). Their setting differs from ours, however, as they artificially increase the feature dimension by aggregating embeddings across the network, while we preserve the native dimensionality of each representation. Therefore, Act has larger dimensionality than the residual stream. To assess whether its larger dimensionality alone explains the gains of Act, we compare it with FC1, which has the same FFN hidden dimension > d. This controlled comparison is on the 307M-parameter variant common to all four model families. As shown in Table 18, overall, Act@100 outperforms FC1@100, with better performance in majority of evaluations. FC1@100 is also subpar compared to the probing baseline RC2@100, indicating that the gains of Act@100 cannot be explained by its larger dimensionality alone.
